newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU pledges to clamp down on 'subsidy shopping'.
newsitem.headline: EU pledges to clamp down on 'subsidy shopping'.

text.p: The European Commission, stung by a controversial plan by French carmaker Renault, said on Friday it was exploring ways of clamping down on a growing trend to relocate business operations in the European Union to take advantage of national and EU subsidies.

"(European Competiton Commissioner Karel) Van Miert will submit a document to the Commission in the following weeks to find out how we can use competition rules to prevent companies from doing what is commonly called 'aid shopping'," Van Miert's spokesman told a news briefing.

The announcement follows the surprise decision by Renault to close a Belgian assembly plant in Vilvoorde and increase production at its northern Spanish subsidiary in Valladolid. Spain on Friday withdrew its plan to subsidise the Valladolid expansion in the face of an angry Brussels reaction.
But the spokesman said the Commission's discussions would have no influence on the Renault move.

This was because the Commission's competition services were only looking into the possibility that some companies were playing off poor European regions which benefit from EU development funds and favourable rules on government subsidies against each other.
Vilvoorde, situated north of Brussels, is not eligible for EU funds. Vallodolid is in the province of Castille-Leon, one of the EU's less developed areas that benefit from EU incentives.

Renault's decision to close its profitable Belgian plant with the loss of 3,100 jobs came only a few days before Spain asked the Commission to clear 11 million European currency units ($12.4 million) in aid to help the French carmaker increase production in Valladolid.
Renault is being accused of flouting Belgian and EU rules on informing and consulting staff on key strategic decisions.
Although The huge row surrounding the affair has cause Spain to suspend the aid request, Renault's Spanish subsidiary said on Friday it would go ahead with the expansion plan.
One further cause for concern at the Commission was the revelation on Friday that EU cash would have gone to Renault's Spanish plant, not just Spanish government money as first thought.
Seven million Ecus ($7.9 million) would have come from the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF), the spokeswoman for Regional Policy Commissioner Monika Wulf-Mathies told reporters.
"We get evidence every day that national authorities cheat; yesterday they had not told us that the ERDF was involved," a Commission official said, commenting on the Spanish request.
Wulf-Mathies's spokeswoman said the Commission would also carry out a thorough reform of its structural funds policy before 1999 to avoid relocation moves.

"We want to promote regional development...but pure profiting from aid needs to be ruled out," the official said speaking on the condition of anonymity. This could be done by making aid conditional on long-term investment. ($1 = 0.883 Ecus)
